Polysemanticity — the condition where a single neuron responds to multiple semantically unrelated features — is not merely an architectural curiosity but a measurement problem with compounding consequences: when you prune a network to increase sparsity, you don't eliminate polysemanticity, you entrench it, because surviving neurons are forced to absorb representational load shed by removed units, collapsing previously distributed features into fewer, more overloaded nodes. The central question is whether progressive pruning fundamentally degrades the disentanglability of learned representations — that is, whether the post-pruning feature geometry becomes irreversibly entangled in ways that defeat sparse dictionary learning methods like sparse autoencoders (SAEs), which assume features occupy recoverable linear subspaces. The key concepts are superposition (Elman 1990; Elhage et al. 2022), where networks represent more features than they have dimensions by exploiting near-orthogonal directions in high-dimensional space; activation sparsity as a precondition for superposition tolerance; and the distinction between incidental polysemanticity (addressable via SAEs) and structural polysemanticity (where features are geometrically fused beyond decomposition). What an expert worries about — and a beginner entirely misses — is that standard pruning criteria (magnitude, gradient sensitivity, activation frequency) are feature-blind: they have no mechanism to prefer neurons whose removal preserves feature disentanglement, so each pruning step silently degrades the SAE's recovery assumptions without any training-time signal flagging the damage. The interpretability breakdown then appears only post-hoc, when mechanistic analysis tools return circuits that are formally coherent but causally misleading — patching experiments succeed on surface behavior while completely misidentifying the underlying computational primitive.
